In formal hardware proof systems, hardware behaviors often need to be described in terms of events that occur over time.  Unfortunately, many such definitions involve a fundamental mistake, specifically that a time limit can run out, leading to nonterminating proofs. This error is highlighted in popular hardware verification tools, specifically in the hardware description language HOL and the BDD-based tool Isabelle/HOL, though it is not unique to them.  This mistake can lead to two serious problems: it may cause tools to crash due to running out of time, and it may appear in verified hardware where it could potentially introduce bugs.  This chapter discusses how to correctly define time limits in HOL, and it provides an easy method for hardware designers to create bounded hardware that will not drop into an infinite loop.  This new definition is not just about adding a bound, but it actually reflects how hardware works, specifically how CPUs have an internal clock that reflects the passage of time.  This chapter also discusses an important property of time limits, specifically that time limits can be translated without affecting the passage of time, and it discusses how this translates into hardware proof tools.  This chapter was written as part of a more extensive collection titled Hardware Verification, and it provides a collection of chapters that explore the more extensive collection. The goal of text classification is to determine a document's category based on its content. Researchers commonly employ a method of converting text into vectors, known as word embeddings, to represent documents in a measurable way. Our research focuses on a specific method, the Synthetic Oversampling technique, and assesses its efficacy in three areas: a) improving accuracy in multi-category text classification, b) achieving accuracy with lower training data sizes, and c) comparing its performance against other oversampling methods. A novel approach using field separation achieves significant speedup for multiphase flow simulations by decomposing high-resolution data into coarse-scale pressure and fine-scale conductivity subproblems. Multiple preconditioners can be used to solve these subproblems, with a Quasi-Compressible Stabilization method and a compressed-lineage formulation boasting optimal convergence and streamlined computation. We evaluate the performance of six combinations of these preconditioners on a challenging flow benchmark featuring intricate porous media structures. Through extensive numerical testing, we identify the most efficient methods and examine how they cope with diverse scenarios, including changing subproblem sizes, subproblem ordering, and subproblem distribution. The results show that a specific combination of subproblems and preconditioners outperforms the others by a large margin, reducing solution times by more than thirty times, and that varying subproblem sizes affects convergence rates, while uneven subproblem distribution may cause uneven solution times. Furthermore, solution times are influenced by the preconditioner used for subproblems, but not by the solution method used for subproblems, and changing the subproblem ordering can speed up computations. The detailed analysis provided in this study should aid in selecting the most suitable field-separated preconditioner setup for specific two-phase flow applications. To build sustainable and resilient urban environments, mayors require accurate, comprehensive, and timely data on city systems. However, mayors often struggle to access unified views of city infrastructure, given that existing databases are typically tailored to specific city departments' or designers' needs. To address this, the GUIDES framework was developed to help cities create and maintain standardized, integrated data systems tailored to mayors' and city administrators' needs. This paper outlines a unified data model and approach for developing a centralized information system and platform, as well as a prototype demonstration based on Chicago, Illinois. The GUIDES core focuses on spatial, transportation, and utility networks, providing a flexible foundation for customizing mayors' access to city infrastructure data. This work presents the core of GUIDES and showcases its potential as a unified information system and platform, paving the way for mayors and city administrators to make more informed decisions by accessing the city's infrastructure in a centralized way. TERS is an emerging technique with great potential for mapping electromagnetic fields within various systems, complemented by chemical analysis, thanks to its unique properties. These include extremely high resolution, the ability to analyze insoluble samples in a neutral state, and a considerable length and width of the probing tip, which enables direct interaction with bulk samples. Although the interaction between the sample and the terahertz radiation is generally weak, it can be pronounced in scenarios with intense electromagnetic fields, charge density waves, or samples with inherent dipole moments. To accurately model and predict the sample's interaction with terahertz radiation, we have developed a comprehensive quantum mechanical method. This method considers the influence of three-field interactions between N-electron, N-orbital, one-dimensional models, and their corresponding vector fields. These include the interactions between the sample's electrons, the electromagnetic fields of the scanning probe, and the terahertz radiation. Our method employs a semiempirical Hamiltonian, derived from the Orlov-Belyaev parametrization, and applies the Hartree-Fock approximation for convenience. To expedite calculations, we have developed a novel algorithm utilizing a binary factorization Woodbury matrix decomposition framework. This method produces a dataset that correlates probe positions, terahertz field amplitudes, and terahertz frequencies with terahertz polarization, dipole moments, and other bulk properties. We have validated our method with a range of test cases, including finite carbon nanotubes, and explored its application to finite graphene and fullerenes. These studies reveal how variations in tube diameter and number of carbon atoms influence electromagnetic fields, ultimately providing a method for quantifying these fields at the nanoscale. However, our method does not consider the complexities of interacting light-matter coupling in the case of small objects, such as nanotubes or fullerenes, where their response to terahertz radiation depends on their orientation with respect to the probe and radiation. This limitation is a critical challenge for working with these systems, and further research is required to overcome it. Nevertheless, our developed quantum mechanical method demonstrates that chemical analysis and electromagnetic field characterization can be seamlessly integrated within the framework of TERS, providing valuable insights into the unique properties of bulk materials at the nanoscale. This method's versatility extends to various types of samples, and it can be applied both as a predictive tool for samples that do not interact strongly with terahertz radiation and as a tool for characterizing samples that do through controlled adjustments to their environment. A thorough investigation of the entropy changes in the two phases of ammonium sulfate ($\left( NH _{4}\right)_{2 }SO _{4 }$) beneath pressure is being conducted. Our study clearly indicates that in the high-temperature phase, an abrupt decrease in entropy, coupled with a positive volume coefficient, occurs at 278 K and 15.58 GPa, aligning with previously reported findings. In contrast, in the low-temperature phase, an opposite trend is observed where entropy gradually decreases as pressure increases. Through density functional theory calculations, it was discovered that at 278 K, the low-temperature phase exhibits intermolecular gaps and a distinct electron cloud, resulting in poor Van der Waals coupling compared to the high-temperature phase. Consequently, disrupting the intermolecular gaps at elevated pressure results in decreased entropy. Furthermore, it was found that at low temperatures, a ferroelectric state exists beyond 3 GPa, characterized by a non-zero polarization value. Our entropic analysis reveals that in the ferroelectric state, an increase in entropy occurs as pressure increases, contrasting with the high-temperature phase. Consequently, the caloric and ferroelectric properties are successfully explained by considering the distinct behaviors of the two phases at various temperature and pressure conditions. Through an electrostatic surface potential analysis, it was determined that alterations in entropy are predominantly influenced by the caloric and ferroelectric states, respectively. Our study also ascertains that in the high-temperature phase, a significant decrease in entropy, coupled with a positive volume coefficient, occurs at 278 K and 15.58 GPa. This finding confirms existing experimental data and highlights the need for further investigation to distinguish between the two phases' behaviors. Overall, our study provides a comprehensive understanding of the entropy changes in the two phases of ammonium sulfate ($\left( NH _{4}\right)_{2 }SO _{4 }$) under pressure. To verify our results, additional experimental data corresponding to varying temperatures and pressures are required. Our study also provides valuable insights for future investigations on the caloric and ferroelectric properties of sulfate salts. It is anticipated that the findings presented here will contribute to a significant advancement in the field of materials science, with particular relevance to pressure-induced caloric and ferroelectric properties. However, the techniques employed by various robotic systems are often in conflict with one another, hindering their potential for collaboration. To resolve these contradictions, we developed a unified approach that enables the seamless integration of diverse robot platforms. This unified framework relies on an automated negotiation system, founded on collective decision-making, allowing the techniques used by individual robots to take effect while promoting collaborative behavior. Our method demonstrates collective autonomy, does not necessitate a priori knowledge of the techniques used by potential collaborators, nor does it require adjustments by the users after a change in the composition of the collaborative group. To verify the effectiveness of our approach, we carried out a series of experiments involving three distinct robot control methodologies, successfully promoting collective behavior in scenarios where the techniques employed by individual robots were in conflict. Additionally, our findings highlight several opportunities for the expansion of our framework. This research offers a solution to incorporate various robot control methodologies within a single framework, providing the foundation for a robust and secure robotic system. Such a system is instrumental in developing an autonomous force, consisting of self-governing robots, capable of working together to yield a significant collective impact. This concept has the potential to bring about a revolution, shifting the world from a state of substantial breakdown to a state of collective prosperity. For tasks involving unfamiliar settings, accurately navigating can be severely hindered by limited cognitive capacity for processing visual information. To address this, a new diagram representation called HiTMap is introduced. Combining the organizational benefits of graphs and topological maps, HiTMap leverages a hierarchical structure to reduce visual information and simplify navigation. By utilizing an unsupervised method to construct a diagram from various map data and incorporating a new class of unsupervised graph metrics called Orientable Perpendicularity, HiTMap is able to optimize its layout and enhance the identification of connected nodes. To evaluate its effectiveness, HiTMap is compared with alternative diagram representations on a range of metrics in a simulated navigation context. Furthermore, HiTMap is applied to real-world scenarios in software development and human-robot interaction. While focusing on indoor spaces, the underlying principles of HiTMap are versatile enough to be extended to navigation in outdoor and non-geographic unfamiliar environments. In the electron gas, gap plasmons arise due to lateral electron movement along a gap between two band gaps. Lateral electron movement triggers both an electron flow away from the gap and an increase in electron density within the gap, which affect plasmon resonance frequencies. When considering infinitesimally narrow gaps, electron density increases without bound, yet the associated energy has no influence on the resonance frequency in the classical electron model. However, according to quantum electrodynamics, an infinitesimally narrow gap would result in an unbounded electromagnetic field energy within the classical electron model, which contradicts the classical outcome. This leads to a modification of the electron density increase, which affects the plasmon resonance frequency. We analyze the electron movement across an infinitesimally narrow gap and its influence on the electromagnetic field energy, ultimately revealing the fundamental source of electron density increases and providing a quantum interpretation of the classical electrodynamics outcome. We compare resonance frequencies in the classical and quantum models and explore scenarios in which the three models converge. Our investigation reveals that a quantum interpretation yields plasmon frequencies distinct from the classical and QED-Dirac models, which may facilitate experimental differentiation between these models. Furthermore, a quantum interpretation may yield infra-red plasmon modes not captured in the classical and QED-Dirac models, opening up new avenues for low-energy electron radiation research. We explore these concepts within the frameworks of nonlocal QED-Dirac and classical electron models. Our study provides a fundamental understanding of the nonlocal electrodynamics influence on low-energy electron radiation and low-energy plasmon modes, which may shed new light on unresolved conflicts within the electron diffusion and radiation theories and the Feynman and Bethe formulas. We discuss potential applications, including electron sources, electron radiation, and particle collisions. We conclude by outlining future research opportunities, including nanoscale electron radiation and plasmon research, and related nanoscale and plasmon research. The conclusion also explores potential implications for an electron monopole emission in the context of the Dirac theory and the chiral bag model of a nucleon. In contextual named entity recovery, we evaluate the significance of individual words for identifying entities. Unlike traditional entity detection tasks, our focus lies within portions of sentences containing gaps in entity labels. This is an unsupervised problem, and we apply techniques from data generation and reinforcement learning to develop contextually-aware models for filling gaps and identifying entities. By generating training data based on expert annotations and using neural models to fill gaps, our approach yields state-of-the-art results on the CoNLL 2003 and 2012 datasets. Additionally, our context-aware model achieves an unsupplied F1 score of 79.36 in the English dataset, and 66.87 in the Spanish dataset. Overall, our goal is to develop models based on limited annotated data that are superior to those of existing contextual word ranking methods. This work is the first to apply reinforcement learning in contextual entity recovery and marks a significant shift away from relying on support vector machine classifiers. Furthermore, our analysis of the recovery process highlights the dynamic nature of term importance between distinct entity recovery tasks. Interestingly, our method produces contrasting importance weights for the same word across different tasks, and within the same task but for different words. One key observation is that nouns related to other nouns tend to be crucial, while those related to pronouns are generally less significant. This raises an important question: What is the underlying story behind recovery patterns of nouns and pronouns, and how do we distill the interplay between them? Analyzing our data reveals that a substantial portion of recovered entities consist of either a single word or two words, and that multi-word entities are often comprised of a pronoun and a noun, confirming prior findings. Moreover, our analysis indicates that a significant number of recovered pronouns are monosyllabic, while single-word entities are predominantly nouns. Importantly, our investigation shows that by combining the analysis of the recovery process and the importance of words, we can uncover the underlying interplay between the two. One key conclusion is that a substantial portion of data provided by the 2012 chemistry dataset can be attributed to the frequent co-occurrence of pronouns and names in the field of chemistry. This highlights a promising direction for enhancing current contextual word ranking models, and our study provides valuable insights for future research in contextual entity recovery. Ultimately, our goal is to develop a flexible model that can be effectively fine-tuned for a variety of entity recovery tasks with minimal adjustments, and our initial examination of the importance of words across distinct tasks indicates that this may be achievable. A developing trend in wireless sensor networks involves using reconfigurable radio devices to switch between frequencies in order to avoid interference and optimize performance. In this context, we explore a specific frequency assignment problem that arises within a part of a reconfigurable sensor network. We analyze a part of the network known as a linear array with multiple nodes and relays. Typically, nodes in the array send data to a central base station through relays, where it is combined into a single signal to increase transmission efficiency. Since power consumption plays a significant role in the network's overall energy usage, we examine how to efficiently distribute power among nodes and schedule relay activation to minimize overall energy usage, while also ensuring data from all nodes reaches the base station. To achieve this, we introduce a planning system that optimizes energy usage, consisting of two interconnected parts. The first part involves selecting which nodes should be active, and which relays should be activated, to ensure data from all nodes reaches the base station. The second part involves determining how much power each node and relay should use, based on the selected activation statuses. By using this planning system, we transform the complex problem of optimizing energy usage, involving a large number of possible activation statuses for nodes and relays, into a more manageable and computationally efficient problem involving only a relatively small number of possible activation statuses. We use an optimization algorithm to find the best possible activation statuses, from which we can then calculate the optimal power consumption of each node and relay, thus completing our planning system. The results we obtained, based on a variety of simulations, confirm that our planning system is highly effective and can reduce energy usage by as much as an order of magnitude, specifically, 90-95%, compared to non-optimized approaches, while maintaining high data transmission success rates to the base station. Building on the success of previous research, a solution has been devised for identifying the edges of cloud formations in geostationary satellite images without utilizing deep networks. The edge detection process utilizes a combination of techniques, including subtracting adjacent images to create a mask that differentiates clouds and non-cloud areas, followed by applying this mask to the original image to isolate the edges of cloud formations. Notably, our approach not only accurately detects cloud edges but also effectively identifies other types of edges within the images, essentially enabling the extraction of edge information for any geometric shape. Furthermore, a method has been implemented to calculate cloud area based on the detected edges, providing a valuable metric for assessing cloud coverage. The approach was successfully tested using images from various satellites in different parts of the world and under various time conditions. Additionally, a case study was conducted to compare and validate our method against a deep network approach, demonstrating comparable performance while also being significantly faster, more transparent, and more adaptable. As a result, the developed technique has been openly sourced and made available for public use, with the authors encouraging continued contributions and improvements to the method through collaborative advances. To model the evolution of primordial black holes in their early stages, we developed a novel, interactive simulation tool, PopSyCLE, which leverages the speed and accuracy of computational mesh relaxation for highly efficient results. We applied a mesh-based approach to study the growth of a black hole in its early stages over a period of 10 billion years, accounting for various factors like surrounding matter, radiation, and collisions with nearby stars. Furthermore, we evaluated how different parameters, such as black hole mass and surrounding matter density, influence the growth of these black holes. In a mesh optimization effort, we compared the efficacy of traditional mesh-based and particle-based methods, ultimately improving PopSyCLE to be at least 5 times more efficient than its previous versions. We also derived a set of benchmark models for testing PopSyCLE, which we applied to study the growth of supermassive black holes. In a further improvement, we employed mesh-based techniques to analyze the optical shadows cast by black holes, as well as the effects of their event horizons, while developing a particle-based method to simulate the distribution of matter around these black holes in accretion scenarios. PopSyCLE's novel mesh-based approach allows for accurate modeling of the growth and properties of supermassive black holes in detail, making it a valuable asset for research and animation purposes. Through our research, we have laid the groundwork for more complex studies of black hole populations and their astrophysical implications, providing insights into a range of cosmological and astrophysical phenomena. Additionally, we have explored the potential for black holes to be used as cosmic probes, allowing us to infer properties of the universe that are not yet directly observable. Furthermore, we have applied PopSyCLE to investigate the possibility that supermassive black holes form from a type of dark matter known as dark shadow matter, rather than through galaxy mergers, enabling us to make testable predictions that could validate or rule out this theoretical model. In a further analysis, we have found that black hole growth is influenced by surrounding matter and radiation, as well as through black hole-star collisions, allowing us to derive a set of efficiency factors that can be used to estimate a black hole's mass based on its event horizon's size. In a related study, we have used PopSyCLE to simulate and analyze a series of black hole models to quantify the effects of their shadows on lensing, as well as their potential for detecting via microlensing, by modeling and analyzing the distribution of light curves produced by black holes in the Milky Way.

By treating the problem as one of non-linear elasticity and applying it to a collection of spherical monomers that compose the wedges, we are able to identify various stages in the process of their deformation. As the monomers slip against one another, the spheres within each wedge change from being in a state of uniform pressure to being in a state of uniform slippage. Using simulations that take into account spherically-shaped obstacles as well as simulations that are based on the classical model of rigidity, we are able to observe not only the transition from one stage to another, but also the point at which the spherical and classical models reach agreement. Ultimately, this agreement occurs at the point at which more than 65% of the spheres within each wedge have undergone slippage. Language models are increasingly being used for downstream tasks such as text classification and machine translation. Traditional fine-tuning methods are resource-intensive and often impractical for production environments. Recent research has explored more efficient fine-tuning techniques like acceleration and injection, which can improve production efficiency. In this paper, we introduce a new acceleration method called PEA, which adapts unique tokens through a pruned attention matrix. Our analysis confirms that PEA remains reliable even with a significantly reduced number of attention heads. Our experiments demonstrate that PEA achieves consistent results with a minimal number of attention heads, producing equivalent performance to full-attention models while significantly reducing computation cost and memory usage. Notably, PEA requires only 1% of the original attention matrix size to produce comparable results on various production datasets, yielding up to a 14x speedup in inference time and a 20x reduction in memory usage. Our code is publicly available on GitHub.

Machine learning model performance enhancement through set augmentation is a widely used technique, however current approaches fail to account for the varying importance of individual examples within a set, leading to inconsistent results. This research proposes the application of contextual preference ordering to address the issue of selecting the most informative data instance within a set, ultimately contributing to the development of more robust augmentation strategies. A neural network implementation of contextual preference ordering is presented, along with experimental validation demonstrating its capability to accurately identify preferred instances, both in settings involving identical and diverse preference relations. Furthermore, a set augmentation method utilizing contextual preference ordering is introduced and evaluated, demonstrating its ability to surpass traditional techniques under both identical and diverse preference relations. Importantly, the proposed method exhibits robust performance across different scenarios, whereas non-contextual preference ordering-based methods struggle with diverse preference relations. In accordance with the experimental design, the code will be made available on GitHub for both the contextual and non-contextual preference ordering implementations, and the set augmentation method will be submitted to the OpenSource Platform. The goal is to facilitate reproducible research and contribute to the development of more informed data augmentation strategies. After conducting multiple iterations of experiments, the paper's findings indicate that contextual preference ordering holds promise for producing more robust set augmentations, especially in complex scenarios featuring diverse preference relations. This research aims to facilitate further exploration of contextual preference ordering within machine learning, ultimately leading to the development of more advanced data augmentation techniques. A system for the automated discovery of contextual preference ordering-based machine learning models is currently under development, for public access on GitHub. Children typically accept whatever they're told, assuming information is accurate, yet they learn to reject unreliable statements over time. In the context of language models, training algorithms can mimic children's initial credulity and subsequent rejection of incorrect information. Researchers have explored various methods for updating the parameters of pre-trained language models, often analogizing these updates to children's growing understanding of truth and falsehood. By reviewing the commonalities and differences between these methods, this work establishes a unified framework, thereby clarifying the underlying techniques and their practical implications. The formalism is applicable to a wide range of transformer-based language models, including both masked and non-masked language models, and has been successfully demonstrated in several critical tasks, including commonsense reasoning, question-answering, and sentiment analysis. The research reveals that the theoretical underpinnings of these methods are well-established, and relevant theoretical contributions are provided. Additionally, an open-source PyTorch code base, named RejPo, has been developed for implementing the proposed methods, and several experimental results are presented that illustrate their effectiveness. The research also identifies potential drawbacks to these methods, and an open challenge is issued to the research community to further investigate and address this concern. The research contributes new knowledge to the field by establishing a clear and comprehensive definition of developmental rejection and its application, and by demonstrating, through empirical results, the effectiveness of this method in several important language tasks. The research's primary findings are: Developmental Rejection can be achieved through Poisson adjustments; The most effective approach involves adjusting not just the head, but the entire transformer; The effectiveness of this method is enhanced when combined with gradient descent; The most successful results are typically obtained through an average of several successful models, rather than relying solely on the most effective model among a set of possibilities; and a potential drawback exists, such that the degree of rejection may be influenced by the quantity to be rejected, rather than the specific content of that quantity. The potential existence of biased sampling is an important area of study, and research is encouraged to further investigate and clarify this concern. The research's theoretical contributions are several key generalizations that provide a unified and comprehensive understanding of the developmental rejection family of algorithms, and their practical implications in the context of the Transformer architecture, and they have the potential to further enhance the performance of language models through the use of the established framework. The research's experimental conclusions are several significant results, and the open-source code and experimental results provided are intended to serve as a resource and reference for the research community. When analyzing text data, experts want more than just machine-predicted outputs; they also want insight into how models arrive at those predictions. In particular, we focus on enhancing the explanatory capabilities of neural machine translation systems by revealing the steps a model takes to translate a sentence. However, existing language generation methods are inherently sequential and do not allow for easy access to this intermediate information. To address this challenge, we propose a novel approach called Look-ahead Focus (LAF) that facilitates explaining model steps during translation by incorporating look-ahead mechanisms into encoder-decoder networks. By utilizing an attention mechanism that looks ahead to future positions, LAF enables several key benefits, including capturing post-focusing translation cues, uncovering focusing decisions made by the model, and providing explicit translation scripts that match human expectations. Experimental results on English-to-French and English-to-German tasks demonstrate that our method improves post-editing quality and significantly reduces the labor involved in post-editing. Furthermore, we conduct an in-depth analysis of LAF's focusing behavior and find that it aligns with expert translation standards. To facilitate future research, we release an updated version of the Neural Machine Translation Explanations dataset, dubbed NME-LAF, which contains relevant examples for studying LAF. Implementing LAF is relatively straightforward, and we provide public code and data to aid researchers and practitioners. Overall, our method represents an important step towards making neural machine translation more transparent and understandable. To the best of our knowledge, our method is the first successful attempt to reveal the focusing decisions of a neural machine translation model. LAF's analysis also sheds light on the utilization of look-ahead mechanisms in other neural language generation methods to uncover the intermediate steps a model takes to generate text. Importantly, our method's ability to use the model's translation history to inform its explanations paves the way for future research into developing look-ahead-based explanation methods for a wide range of text generation tasks. Implementing LAF requires modifying only one layer of the encoder-decoder network, and we release public code and data, including a refined version of the Neural Machine Translation Explanations dataset, to aid researchers and practitioners. This note issues a critical warning regarding a recently published research article that employs an incorrect assumption about linear transformations within the author's own defined mathematical framework. As proven in the companion paper \cite{2020arXiv19011113}, it was found that this framework lacks the requisite properties necessary for preserving linear relationships. Consequently, the main contribution of the referenced article is invalidated. Furthermore, this notification also aims to provide a concise and accessible description of affine transformations, as well as an alternative solution to the original problem proposed in the contested article by incorporating a novel affine structure introduced in \cite{2020arXiv19011113}. The work presented here is primarily focused on addressing the methodological flaws present in the criticized article and does not intend to diminish the author's initial contributions to the field. We suggest that the methodological improvements presented here be integrated in a revised version of the original article to prevent the propagation of incorrect methods and to promote the dissemination of the original results to a wider audience. The methodological improvements described here also serve to further advance the research goals outlined in the contested article. Specifically, the final section of this notice explores an enhanced solution to the original problem and derives a concise, semi-analytical formula expressing the expected price that would result from paying a fixed Asian rate on an Asian option. Visual representations learned by a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) are difficult to decipher but are crucial for the network's performance. Previous research aimed at visualizing CNN representations discovered that some features are easy to recognize but others are obscure. Prolonged training in higher semantic abstractions enables deeper CNN representations, but it's unclear how these representations correspond to image details. We found that our novel visualization technique, Latent Visual-Semantic Evaluation (LVSE), yields a more coherent and easier to understand set of features. We discovered that our Coherent Filter Bank, extracted using LVSE, is resistant to noise and retains its organization, unlike other methods. Additionally, we developed a semantic where we identify distinct image regions using LVSE, a task previously considered impossible. Our research indicates that higher abstract representations in CNNs correspond to simplified, conceptual feature representations, whereas lower-level representations correspond to distinct image elements. Our findings support the Coherent Representational Invariance hypothesis, which state that CVR network representations are both coherent and versatile. Our results can be viewed on our website: https://filterbanks.github.io. The code and data are available at https://github.com/githubfs/LVSE. As such, CVR networks can effectively learn a wide range of semantic concepts that correspond to meaningful image features, a talent shared by humans. Importantly, our research facilitates the systematic evaluation of the interpretation of deep neural networks. Future research should focus on additional methods for systematically evaluating the interpretation of deep neural networks. The internal module of the adversarial module categorizes inputs, dividing them into distinct clusters based on their probability distributions, and fits a separate adversarial module to process each group. The outputs from these modules are combined to form the ground truth for classification, with which the transversal module is trained to generate the desired outputs. Modeling complex geodynamo and solar dynamo through mean-field frameworks offers a convenient approach, breaking down key processes into magnetohydrodynamics equations and additional equations governing the interactions between magnetic fields and velocity fields. Research has primarily relied on a limited scope of "magnetohydrodynamics for astrophysicists," incorporating only one type of turbulent influence, which fails to account for crucial global effects, such as those seen in el-Nadi et al. 2020. We present a more comprehensive framework that includes a full spectrum of turbulent influences, which leads to solutions that align more closely with those of direct numerical simulations, particularly in the presence of weak magnetic fields. This model allows for self-consistent solutions that do not rely on unrealistic assumptions and helps to explain how Earth's and other stars' internal magnetic fields develop. Our model serves as a foundation for creating a global geodynamo model that can be used to investigate various parameters and processes, similar to previous models. However, our model does not require adjusting eddy viscosity and eddy diffusivity parameters, indicating that these parameters are not well-defined. Additionally, we demonstrate that incorporating the geostrophic degeneracy into mean-field frameworks results in a non-unique solution for the mean magnetic field's growth timescale, which provides further insights into the complex dynamics involved in the geodynamo and astrophysical dynamos, as described in an accompanying discussion. Further investigation is needed to fully understand these complex dynamics and the importance of certain parameters. Investors often assess their wealth in relation to others as a means of measuring success. To capture this relative assessment, we use a function that combines an investor's absolute wealth with the ratio of their wealth to the total wealth of a target group. This relative wealth measure is applied to various scenarios, including when the target group consists solely of the investor or when it comprises the investor and multiple other individuals. By maximizing the expected value of this relative wealth measure within a defined time frame, we conduct a thorough analysis. This analysis involves solving two distinct stochastic control problems. The first problem is related to a family partnership, where multiple investors co-own a portfolio, and the solution involves optimizing portfolio management with a performance benchmark that compares each investor's wealth to the total wealth of the partnership. The second problem explores a situation, where multiple investors are separate individuals, and the solution involves optimizing portfolio management using a performance benchmark that compares each individual's wealth to the total wealth of the partnership, normalized by the total wealth. To solve these problems, we employ a unique method of differentiating the logarithm of the relative wealth process, and then we verify the applicability of these approaches through concrete examples, including a single investor and a partnership consisting of two investors. The results enable us to compare the traditional mean-variance optimization strategy, where success is measured solely by absolute wealth, with two relatively measured optimization strategies, and demonstrate the impact of different benchmarks on the structure of the optimal portfolio management policies. To validate these approaches, we conduct a numerical analysis of a model with stochastic market prices, and demonstrate that the derived policies can effectively influence market trends. To further illustrate the practical implications of these findings, we also provide a case study of real-world portfolio management. The analysis reveals that the shape of the performance function plays a significant role in determining the optimal portfolio management strategy, and using a performance function with a sharp increase at the low end can lead to a higher M^2/H^2 ratio, indicating greater market sensitivity, and may result in a lower portfolio risk and higher return. Conversely, using a performance function with a slow increase at the high end can lead to a lower M^2/H^2 ratio, lower portfolio risk, and lower return. Ultimately, the choice of the performance function depends on the specific investment goals of the individual or group. The derived methods for optimizing portfolio management strategies have been successfully tested in various practical situations, and the resulting policies have been verified through numerical analysis and example applications. Diminutive galaxies, with sizes less than $10^{9}$ solar masses, are difficult to study as their characteristic bright central black holes and young, luminous stars make it hard to spot the less luminous underlying galactic components. Further analysis of the data, which was done using a unique statistical approach, suggested that diminply galaxies' intergalactic media contain a notable amount of hot gas that is in excess of what would be found in massive galaxies' intergalactic media. Researchers were unsure of the exact cause of this result, but they presented several potential explanations. One possibility is that diminply galaxies' intergalactic media are heated by feedback from their central black holes, which would result in less heated gas due to smaller black holes. Another possibility is that diminply galaxies' intergalactic media are heated by galaxy interactions, which would result in more extensive heating. By comparing data from a particular sample of galaxy clusters, researchers found that diminply galaxies' intergalactic media are not as hot as those found in galaxy clusters. Additionally, researchers could investigate the intergalactic media of more massive diminply galaxies to see if there are any correlation between galaxy mass and intergalactic media temperature. Such a study could result in a significant advancement in our understanding of diminply galaxies and their intergalactic media. This paper introduces an original variant of the sweeping motion equation known as the "ig-sweep" dynamical system. This new equation is derived from a specific type of inequality involving mean values and is characterized by two key factors: a measure defined within an evolving set $D\subset\mathbb{R}^N}$ and with an added constraint involving its boundary $\partial D$. We establish existence and uniqueness results for this new dynamical system through a combination of two main methods: first by proving that its flow is continuous and well-defined, and second by demonstrating that solutions to ig-sweep motions are also solutions to a corresponding variational inequality. Furthermore, we create a new model that combines the principles of elastic shocks from continuing flows and elastic collisions in continua, thereby facilitating deformation processes in continua with moving boundaries. Lastly, we develop another variant of the ig-sweep equation by incorporating an additional factor: a measure defined within the boundary layers of evolving sets $\partial D\subset\mathbb{R}^N}$. This new variant is derived from a specific type of inequality involving tangential values and is characterized by two key factors: a normal vector field to the boundary $\partial D$ and an added constraint involving its boundary layers $\partial\partial D$. We establish that solutions to ig-sweep motions with layer subproblems are also solutions to a corresponding variational inequality, and finally, we present an application of the ig-sweep equation to a model for granular materials with elastic shocks and inelastic collisions. We enrich the proposed model with an added layer of fragmentation, thereby facilitating deformation processes in continua with elastic shocks and inelastic collisions, and we further demonstrate the emergence of plastic shocks that adhere to a specific type of plastic potential function when solutions to the proposed model are also solutions to a corresponding subdifferential inequality. Ultimately, the ig-sweep equation provides a wealth of new dynamic models with diverse applications across various fields. Built upon the established KKMC program for leptons and QCD processes, KKMCee extends the capabilities to include the accurate description of non-resonant multi-photon production in both initial-state radiations and final-state radiations. The insertion deaths technique is implemented to provide a complete description of pair production, complemented by the implementation of the tevatron working group benchmark tasks. With the integration of the EERTS2 electroweak corrections module, KKMCee offers a comprehensive set of five and six photon amplitudes for lepton pairs, along with state-of-the-art hadronic and semi-hadronic decays for both lepton and quark pairs. The tool also offers an option for post-generation off-shell smearing, allowing users to model exact Higgs or top quark off-shell production in future colliders. The tool's features include an interface with the DELPHES fast simulator and the presentation of benchmark tasks from the Tevatron and HL-LHC collaborations. The performance of KKMCee is showcased through a detailed description of one-loop $2y$ corrections for the weak boson mass in known heavy flavor insertions. The tool successfully reproduces the sensitivity of the $2y$ correction to the $W$ mass in a HL-LHC environment through a comparison with the established HEPFAST Monte Carlo event generator. The output of KKMCee matches the one from HEPFAST@LHC to one part in $10^{5}$. Furthermore, the tool accurately describes the $2\beta$ correlation function for fermion pairs, complemented by the implementation of the insertion deaths technique to provide a complete description of pair production in future leptonic colliders. The output of KKMCee successfully reproduces the pair production cross sections for various benchmark scenarios at the ILC and CLIC colliders. The tool's performance is comparable to the one of KKMC, with the former successfully describing the dominant contribution to pair production in future leptonic colliders. As these groups worked to identify and contact potential contacts of infected individuals, opportunities arose for collaborative efforts to be made, enabling the sharing of data and thereby enhancing the overall tracing process. This research aims to evaluate the advantages of engaging in regional tracing collaborations from a mathematical perspective, using an epidemiological model to simulate the virus transmission in different scenarios. Specifically, we analyze the influence of regional collaborations on the transmission dynamics of COVID-19 in England by developing and comparing model variants representing individual actions in the absence of collaboration and collective decisions during collaboration, and subsequently determine key metrics that indicate the efficacy of contact tracing efforts. Through thorough numerical analysis, our findings reveal that regional tracing collaborations can lead to a notable decrease in the number of identified contacts per infected individual, an improvement of up to 7.94%, and also result in a more even distribution of infections across different contact categories, while simultaneously reducing the time it takes for a case to generate new infections, resulting in an increase of up to a 10% in transmission speed. Additionally, our research also identifies potential collaboration scenarios in which the virus transmission can be completely eliminated. This work is further validated by comparing its predictions to real-world data related to the traceability of COVID-19 in England, as reported by the National Health Service, NHS Test and Trace, Test, Trace, and Public Health England. Following thorough analysis of these results, our model is used to make some general predictions regarding the influence of the tracing collaborations on the transmission dynamics of COVID-19 and also provide recommendations for future tracing efforts, as informed by our findings. Currently, ensuring this validation involves extensive mathematical proofs, checkpointing data, or independent third-party calculations, all of which are highly resource-intensive and often impractical. In this paper, we explore an alternative approach, which utilizes a mistake-assessment technique for physics-based neural networks. This technique, which we've dubbed 'Posterior Validation', enables us to verify that a network's predictions remain accurate even after they've been created, without needing access to ground truth data, by leveraging the underlying physical model and existing checkpoint data. Our method is demonstrated on a variety of problems, including a simplified version of the Euler equations, before being applied to more complex problems involving partial differential equations in multiple dimensions. Our research indicates that PPNs with Posterior Validation are just as accurate as those with ground truth training and can be just as effective at detecting mistakes in networks. Our method is simple, requires only additional checkpointing, and can be used on existing PPNs without needing to retrain them. This makes it a promising approach for validating complex systems like turbulent flows and confirmatory biology and medical simulations. Additionally, we've adapted our method for real-time validation and testing, allowing for more robust safety critical applications, even if it's not feasible to store all checkpoint data. Our code has been made available on GitHub. One potential limitation of our approach is that it relies on having accurate checkpoint data, which may not always be available. Furthermore, our method assumes that the Posterior Validation loss is a reliable measure of a network's accuracy, although this may not always be the case, leading to false positives in certain situations. Our work is an initial step towards developing verifiable and reliable machine learning models, but there are still limits to what we can currently achieve. Future research could potentially address these limitations and expand the range of applicable data. Ultimately, our method offers a promising avenue for increasing the confidence we have in AI-generated predictions in fields like physics and engineering. Although we primarily focused on physics-based neural networks, our technique could potentially be applied more broadly to other areas, including computer vision and natural language processing. One potential extension of our work would be to develop Posterior Validation for these more general models, allowing for greater reliability across a wider range of applications. The evaluation of musical compositions has long been a contentious issue in music information retrieval. While music theorists evaluate compositions by considering multiple aspects, no clear definition exists for what constitutes a great musical piece, making the development of an automated evaluation method highly desirable. This study successfully applies techniques for evaluating the quality of generated music to the evaluation of composed music. To achieve this, we first defined key aspects of musical composition and identified relevant words from a substantial collection of musical pieces. A transformer-based language model was used to calculate the similarity between words and compositions, and the results were normalized to allow comparisons of compositions. Normalized values for various compositions of different lengths were also calculated. Analysis of the results revealed the importance of certain words and compositional aspects, and highlighted the difficulties of learning metrics for compositions of significantly different lengths. Further experiments involved the comparison of various transformer models and the impact of training data. The study's findings provided insights into the distinct characteristics of various famous composers. Interestingly, our results indicated that Bach's music was characterized by words such as'simple','short', or'repeating', whereas the music of Mozart was described as 'complex', 'long', or 'innovative'. This research marks the first attempt at using transformer-based models to evaluate musical compositions as a whole. The study's outcomes may lead to further applications, such as using transformer-based models to generate or evaluate musical patterns, for example the development of autogenous music or the evaluation of the quality of generated music. However, significant challenges remain to be overcome before such applications can be effectively implemented. Potential future research directions are also explored in this study. To enhance the resilience of NLP models in face of language manipulation, we introduce a novel concept of sibylvariant models. Built upon the ideas of adversarial variants and robustness in machine learning, sibylvariant models represent NLP models with varying viewpoints or interpretations of the same training data. To demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach, we develop sibylvariant modifications for SVMs, leveraging different sorting algorithms, and test them on four text classification datasets. The results show that sibylvariant models exhibit consistent performance and can be utilized to mitigate out-of-distribution prediction issues, protect models against adversarial attacks and data poisoning, and reduce dependence on a single training dataset. Furthermore, we propose a method for creating a sibylvariant ensemble using conformal prediction, enabling more accurate text classification and out-of-distribution detection with models that are resilient to changing environments. The findings and code for our research are made publicly available. Ultimately, the idea of sibylvariant models has the potential to significantly contribute to the development of NLP models that are adaptable and resilient in dynamic language contexts. 

Please note that this research focuses primarily on text classification and the principles of sibylvariant models rather than attacking neural networks, and as such it does not involve any forms of model inversion or other forms of attacks that have been discussed in related research. Our work builds on existing concepts of adversarial variants and the idea of promoting robust machine learning learning trajectories. In the realm of NLP, sibylvariant models represent a new and important area of study.

In total, six sibylvariant modifications were developed for the purposes of this research.

Utilizing pruning, quantization, and knowledge distillation techniques can help decrease model size and improve computational efficiency, making low-resource machine translation more feasible. Results show that utilising knowledge distillation with a 1-bit quantized teacher significantly outperforms using a full-precision teacher, with negligible quality loss when appropriately implemented. Compared to other compression methods, distillation with a quantized teacher exhibits superior performance and efficiency, making it an attractive solution for low-resource MT settings. With ongoing advancements in hardware and software, it is anticipated that efficient models such as those obtained by distilling a quantized teacher will play a significant role in low-resource MT settings in the future. This includes scenarios like zero-shot MT and low-resource language pairs. The detection of pneumonia through automated segmentation of affected areas is critical for timely diagnosis and treatment, yet relies on manual labeling for model training - an impractical task given the current scarcity of medical experts and imaging data. We investigate the potential of image enhancement techniques to decrease the amount of labeled data needed for high-quality pneumonia segmentation. We evaluated several image processing methods, including anisotropic diffusion, unsharp masking, and unet segmentation models with a Gaussian blur. Our experiments involved using enhanced images from both real and artificially created datasets, which produced results comparable to the use of 1000 natural images, with improvements achieved with as little as a 10% augmentation. Notably, some image processing methods were able to match the segmentation quality of a model trained on 1000 augmented images, equaling the performance of a model trained on 2000 natural images. These results suggest that image processing methods can greatly reduce the amount of data needed for high-quality pneumonia segmentation, whether using augmented or natural images, thereby making medical image analysis more feasible even in data-scarce environments. Furthermore, our approach is versatile and can be applied to various tasks beyond generating image descriptions, thus paving the way for future studies to utilize our approach on a broader range of applications. We anticipate that our research will inspire future work to develop more descriptive and coherent image descriptions that are reminiscent of human language. We propose Zero-shot Voice Interpretation, a task that enables a model to convey
the content of spoken audio without requiring training on specific categories.
Our approach involves a unified framework for audio analysis, concept representation,
and a association mechanism that connects words to abstract ideas. On the audio front,
we design an architecture that extracts meaningful segments from spoken audio.
Our experiments based on the YAMNet feature extractor extract general audio patterns
instead of specific entities, compromising ZSVI performance. To overcome this, we suggest
using the VGGtradV5 feature extractor, often used for speaker recognition and verification.
Our re-examinations using the updated extractors demonstrate the ZSVI method's potential
with the correct choice of audio processing pipeline. Building on existing solutions
significantly reduces ZSVI-closed domain accuracy from 51.95 to 67.14 and ZSVI-domain-neutral
accuracy from 10.27 to 16.57. Our findings indicate that audio processing is a critical
component of ZSVI, and further research is needed to tackle the challenging task of
identifying abstract ideas from spoken words without prior training. By combining
state-of-the-art models for audio segmentation, concept association, and speech interpretation,
we achieve satisfactory results, and a complete model code along with dataset is
available at https://github.com/dkowalski/zeroshot-voice-interpretation. The related
video can be watched at https.//youtu.be/7KXG2Yk_7Gw. The model's audio demonstrations

Building on work by Coleman and Gurtin, who introduced a theory of heat flow through materials with memory, this paper extends their ideas to a system consisting of an interior region and a boundary with its own internal structure. The interior follows a standard heat equation, while the boundary is modeled after a similar equation but with reduced heat conductivity and a unique generation term related to the boundary's stored energy. A related initial and boundary value problem is posed, and we demonstrate the local existence and uniqueness of solutions under minimal assumptions. Furthermore, we establish the continuous dependence of solutions on key problem data. To illustrate these new equations, we consider specific examples including hyperbolic heat flow on a solid's surface and a model featuring thermocouples coupled with a material possessing internal energy memory. We verify the well-posedness of these models by carefully selecting the problem data's source terms. Additionally, this paper derives a first-order linearized system for small disturbances, as well as its continuous and positive definite energy estimates, to showcase the robust behavior of these thermodynamic systems. Finally, we present examples including surface phase transitions and a model of heat propagation through a solid with internal defects. We observe that for surface defects described using distributional derivatives, the generated surface energy is vast for large distances and the surface wave equation becomes an acoustical wave, while for smaller distances, the surface energy is vast again, but this time the surface wave equation represents damped wave behavior. We attribute this behavior to the surface wave experiencing energy loss due to memory effects. We note that these models can be extended to higher dimensions, leading to the description of their spectral properties. We leave the exploration and modeling of more complex systems for future studies. We believe that these new equations, which account for the behavior of materials with memory, are a valuable tool for mathematical modeling and analysis. By extending the work of Coleman and Gurtin, we aim to further understand the behavior of systems with memory and their potential applications in both mathematics and engineering. We also leave several potential research paths for the future, including the modeling and analysis of systems consisting of multiple connected regions, the surface growth of materials through boundary stretching, and the introduction of systems of measure-valued solutions to account for the potential loss of memory when dealing with internal defects and fringes. We believe that these topics offer an exciting opportunity for further research and collaboration. For each interaction point, recommended best practices are provided, including relevant literature and empirical knowledge. Breast computed tomography allows for early detection of COVID-19, but standard image analysis is complicated by significant noise and uneven illumination, making it difficult to accurately pinpoint tumors. Due to the labor-intensive process of manually labeling tumor locations, we developed an innovative, efficiently guided learning technique to automatically identify lung abnormalities in BCT scans. By initially training a model using lung masks to locate general tumor areas, and then refining it with post-contrast enhancement images to segment the abnormalities, we achieved high precision in analyzing these scans, thus contributing a new approach for completely automated tumor detection and segmentation, particularly effective in analyzing BCT scans. Experimental results show that our technique significantly surpasses other recent methods in both accuracy and speed, yielding an average dice coefficient of approximately 0.90 and an average box IoU of around 0.85. The technique also demonstrates considerable speed advantages, taking only a fraction of the time required by other methods, reducing training time by a notable margin. Accurate vertebra labeling is crucial in spine-related medical analysis and treatment planning. This task typically requires skilled radiologists to identify and match C7, L1, and other vertebrae to calculate heights, orientations, and pitches. A significant challenge arises from variable and distinctive vertebral shapes and landmarks. To streamline this process, an automated vertebra labeling method is developed, addressing positioning and recognition combined. This technique involves first correcting spinal distortions, then extracts and represents vertebra contours in a 2D plane to calculate their positions and orientations. Due to significant T1-L2 shape variations, vertebra recognition relies on anatomically constrained optimization, using recognized C7 and L1 as references to identify the remaining vertebrae through a multi-resolution strategy. This optimization is based on feature similarity and is adapted to balance robustness and sensitivity. To improve accuracy, anatomical characteristics and general features are combined in a weighted sum. This vertebral recognition method is unique, combining positioning and recognition, and more robust to shape and landmark variations. To assess its effectiveness, extensive clinical testing has been conducted, demonstrating that this technique can calculate vertebra positions and orientations with high accuracy, and that the recognition rate exceeds 98% for a large dataset of 50 CT scans. This research has significant implications for the development of spinal analysis and treatment planning software. The effectiveness of soft actuators in robotic systems is well-established, 
but their application in locomotion systems remains understudied. We used 
inverted pendulum-based quadruped locomotion, combining it with elastic aid, 
to explore the capabilities of soft actuators. We developed five distinct 
actuator configurations, each with a unique hard-soft balance, to determine 
how impact resistance affects mobility. Through open-loop tests, we identified 
that a specific'sweet spot' exists where additional softness in the actuator 
does not hinder performance, using simulation models that learn this connection 
between softness and mobility. When this model was applied in real-world 
experiments, it accurately predicted the effects of actuator configurations on 
quadruped mobility, showing that soft actuators enhance system performance, 
as long as their elasticity is properly harnessed. Our research lays the 
groundwork for controlling elastic actuators in mobility systems, allowing them 
to lower costs, enhance system resilience, and improve efficiency. The models

The issue of divisibility in quantum dynamics has seen various recent analyses from a positive map perspective, which essentially rephrases the problem into an optimization task, thereby allowing the application of techniques such as the maximum likelihood principle and Bayesian inference. By introducing a variational approach, researchers have discovered that the best achievable states under these conditions are continuous and, in certain cases, exactly attainable. This new method has been successfully applied to three prominent non-commuting quantum systems - the Rabi model, an SU(1,1) spin-cutoff model, and an SU(N)-parameterized model. It has been found that the Rabi model, in particular, exhibits full divisibility, whereas the other models only achieve partial divisibility. Furthermore, the model parameters have been optimized to demonstrate the possibility of reaching the Birkhoff cone's interior for both the SU(1,1) and SU(N) models. We observe that our findings for the Rabi model align with existing Monte Carlo simulations and both semi-classical and quantum reduced dynamics calculations. We have also applied reduced dynamics to model the interaction between a two-level system and a scalar light mode within the Rabi model, only to discover that full divisibility allows for a well-defined, unambiguous entropy increase. We have derived a closed-form expression of the optimal map for the Rabi model and believe that scaling our variational method to larger systems could provide valuable insights in the study of quantum dynamics and quantum information processing. This research focuses on utilizing trait-based fashion search, distinguishing it from standard image retrieval approaches. A key challenge arises from the lack of data and the requirement to define traits, followed by the difficulty of pinpointing images with specific features. Existing algorithms often neglect these issues or simplify them by relying on limited supervision or trait definitions. Furthermore, adjusting an image's feature is typically an intricate process, necessitating deep understanding of fashion and semantics. We address these problems by introducing a novel supervised technique for identifying images according to defined traits in the fashion industry. A dataset of human annotations for key fashion attributes has been collected, allowing us to develop a simple yet effective approach for feature-level search. Although initially designed for basic retrieval, our proposed method, FFA-Net, can also accommodate more sophisticated requirements such as semi-automatic feature manipulation and semi-supervised training. FFA-Net leverages an innovative architecture to search for trait-defined features and uses a novel feature-level attribute assignment method to boost search accuracy. Through a combination of hard example mining and soft feature alignment, FFA-Net's performance is enhanced, achieving top results in the FashionRT benchmark. Notably, FFA-Net's semi-supervised version exhibits exceptional performance with minimal training data, outshining other popular supervised and unsupervised algorithms in the benchmark. Importantly, FFA-Net enables semi-automatic feature-level trait definition and image retrieval, expanding its applications to a broader range of scenarios. Finally, FFA-Net's ability to perform feature-level attribute assignment facilitates the design of novel supervised attribute assignment methods. Empirical evaluations demonstrate that FFA-Net's performance in fashion search and attribute assignment surpasses existing state-of-the-art algorithms. Evaluating the depth in light field images is complex due to their intrinsic properties. Most existing methods focus solely on surface depth, whereas their performance degrades in scenarios of occlusion. We present a novel, versatile approach that effectively leverages occlusion to accurately estimate depth in light field images. Our novel metric is derived from the optimal angular sampling patterns, which it identifies within images featuring occlusion. This approach is then tested on various practical applications, such as depth estimation, light field-based depth rendering, and light field-based stereo matching. Notably, our method surpasses state-of-the-art techniques in all these applications. Our study sets forth a comprehensive understanding of how occlusion aids in accurate light field depth estimation.
